title: Designing Silk-silk Protein Alloy Materials for Biomedical Applications
protocol: Visit the National Center for Biotechnology Information website.
Search for "fibroin [Antheraea pernyi]" to find amino acid sequences for protein A.
Save the amino acid sequence of fibroin [Antheraea pernyi].
Search for "fibroin heavy chain precursor [Bombyx mori]" and "fibroin light chain precursor [Bombyx mori]" for protein B.
Save the amino acid sequences of fibroin heavy chain precursor and fibroin light chain precursor from Bombyx mori.
Visit the ExPASy website or use other commercial software to calculate basic bioinformatics data for proteins based on their sequences.
Include total charge per molecule, hydrophobicity index, and titration curve at different pH values in the analysis.
Use this information as elements for computational simulation of protein interactions.
Determine whether the two proteins have strong interactions through the simulations.
Verify the protein alloy system by an experimental method described in step 3.1 using precise thermal analysis.
Simulate the protein alloy system using a lattice-spring-mass (LSM) model.
Write a simulation program in C programming language for single or multiprocessor computer systems.
Represent each protein as a coarse-grained particle with mass m.
Use Hookean or neo-Hookean springs to represent bonds between particles.
Interlink a finite number of particles with springs to create stable sub-alloy domains.
Assign different spring constants to represent various bond types within and between sub-alloys.
Model the protein alloy system as a material composed of crosslinked sub-alloy domains.
Use the Bell Model to simulate bond breaking and reformation processes.
Allow weak bonds to reform while preventing strong bonds from reforming once broken.
Apply external forces equally to each particle in the system when solving the force equation using Newton’s Laws.
Model interactions between water molecules and proteins by applying an additional drag force to each particle.
Solve the force equation for each particle considering the spring force from bonds, external force, and frictional force.
Calculate and extract the positions of protein particles as a function of time.
Calculate physical quantities that characterize alloy-proteins from the positions of the particles.
Change the bond stiffness in the program to understand interactions between different proteins.
Cut raw wild tussah silk cocoons or fibers at a weight of 3 g.
Measure 3 g of sodium dicarbonate or sodium carbonate.
Fill a 2 L glass beaker with distilled water.
Place the glass beaker on a hot stage, cover it with aluminum foil, and heat to boiling.
Remove the aluminum foil cover and slowly add the measured sodium dicarbonate into the boiling water, allowing it to completely dissolve.
Add raw protein fibers (wild silk fibers) into the boiling water and allow them to boil for 2-3 hours.
Carefully remove the protein fibers from the solution with a spatula after boiling.
Squeeze the removed fibers to remove excess water.
Immerse fibers in a 2 L beaker with cold distilled water.
Wash fibers twice for 30 min each to remove impurities.
Dry fibers in a fume hood for at least 12 hr.
Melt 45.784 g of calcium nitrate in a glass beaker at 65 °C.
Combine fibers and solvent at a ratio of 1 g fiber into 10 ml solvent.
Dissolve fibers at 95 °C for 5 to 12 hr.
Inject the wild silk solution into dialysis cassettes or sealed dialysis tubings using syringes.
Dialyze against 2 L of distilled water, changing water frequently (after 30 min, 2 hr, 6 hr, and then every 12 hr for 3 days).
After 3 days, collect the protein solutions from the dialysis cassettes or tubing.
Place the collected solutions into 13,000 rpm rated tubes.
Centrifuge the solutions for 1 hour at 3,500 rpm at 4 °C.
Repeat centrifugation three times to remove deposits.
Quickly transfer the supernatant into new tubes after each run.
Store the final solutions in a 4 °C refrigerator.
Pour 5 ml of protein solution onto a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) substrate or other flat hydrophobic substrate.
Allow the protein solution to dry completely, which typically takes more than 12 hours.
Weigh the remaining solid protein film after drying.
Calculate the final solution concentration by weight percentage: Measured Weight (in mg) ÷ 5 (in ml) ÷ 10.

Collect another selected natural protein fiber and repeat the above process with an appropriate “soap” and dissolving solvent until obtaining a final protein water solution with measured concentration.
Dilute Protein A in distilled water at 4°C to form a 1.0 wt% Protein A aqueous solution.
Dilute Protein B in distilled water at 4°C to form a 1.0 wt% Protein B aqueous solution.
Slowly mix the 1 wt% protein A solution with the 1 wt% protein B solution at 4°C using a pipette to avoid protein aggregation during mixing.
Mix pure protein A and protein B solutions as controls.
Calculate the mixing volume ratio for a specified molar ratio of Protein A:Protein B by Volume A:Volume B = R·(MW of A): (100-R)·(MW of B).
Immediately cast the final solutions onto PDMS substrates to form films or other designed materials.
Do not store high concentration protein alloy solutions for a long time.
Dilute the blend solutions with ion-free distilled water if needed, and keep them in a 4 °C refrigerator to avoid additional protein aggregation in solutions.
Prepare PDMS substrates and clean them by soaking in distilled water.
Cast the protein blend solutions with different mixing ratios onto the PDMS substrates.
Dry the solutions for at least 12 hours in a chemical hood with air flow until films are formed.
Use the same volume for different solutions so that the thickness of films can be fixed.
Remove the protein alloy films from the PDMS substrates and place them onto clean dishes.
Weigh many Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) aluminum pans and lids for DSC study.
Match the pan and lid pairs to have an equal total weight.
Encapsulate 6 mg of each type of dried protein blend into aluminum DSC pans.
Seal an empty pan and lid pair for use as the reference.
Calibrate the DSC instrument with sapphire and indium for heat flow and temperature, respectively.
Pre-run the DSC at a heating rate of 2 K/min to 150 °C.
Hold the pre-run sample at 150 °C for 15 min to remove water molecules.
Cool down the pre-run sample quickly (10 K/min) to 25 °C.
Run the DSC again at a heating rate of 2 K/min to 300 °C or until the degradation peak appears.
Record the heat capacities of the protein samples during this process.
Change the old sample in the DSC to a new sample with a different mixing ratio.
Calculate Heat Capacity vs. Temperature curves for each protein blend sample using DSC software.
Judge miscibility of protein blends by examining individual single glass transition temperatures Tg(A) and Tg(B).
Determine if proteins are fully miscible based on intermediate single glass transition temperature between Tg(A) and Tg(B).
Identify immiscible phase separation blends if both Tg(A) and Tg(B) appear at original positions with step heights proportional to composition.
Recognize semi-miscible composite blends by observing one broad or two migrated glass transitions closer together than pure protein components.
Produce or purchase a designed topographic surface for casting.
Place the glass with diffraction patterns into a dish, patterned side upward.
Mix PDMS solution in a 9:1 ratio of potting and catalyst solutions.
Spread the PDMS solution evenly on the glass surface to cover all patterns.
Place the casting dish in a 65 °C oven for at least 2 hours on a flat surface.
Remove the PDMS substrate from the glass after drying.
Punch out PDMS molds with diffraction patterns using a suitable hole punch.
Drop protein alloy solutions onto the PDMS surfaces with diffraction patterns.
Dry the films containing protein alloy solutions for at least 12 hours.
Place dry films and PDMS molds into a 60 °C vacuum oven (25 kPa) with water dish on the bottom of the chamber.
Pump out air in the oven, let water vapors anneal samples for at least 2 hours.
Release the vacuum and peel off the water insoluble film from the PDMS substrate using forceps.
Test quality of diffraction patterns on films by comparing them with original patterns on glass.
Clean a glass slide using Alconox in an ultrasonic cleaner for 5 min.
Clean the glass slide using acetone for 5 min.
Clean the glass slide using methanol for 5 min.
Blow the glass slide dry using dry nitrogen gas.
Introduce substrate materials into the deposition chamber.
Evacuate the loadlock to a pressure of 30 mTorr.
Open the gate valve between the loadlock and main deposition chamber.
Turn on the Ar gas and adjust the pressure regulator to the desired deposition pressure.
Pre-sputter for several minutes to remove oxide layers and contaminants from the target.
Open the shutter and sputter metal onto the substrate using an RF power of 100 W.
Remove the coated glass slide from the chamber.
Using a spinner, spin a photoresist coating onto the surface of the film.
Soft bake at 90 °C for 5 min to dry the resist.
Place a contact mask with an image of the device firmly against the resist.
Expose the photoresist using a UV light source for 10 sec.
Place the film in the photoresist developer until the projected image appears.
Dip the film in DI water to stop the developer from working on the unexposed photoresist.
Blow the films dry with dry nitrogen gas.
Place the films into an oven at 120 °C for 15 min to hard bake the photoresist.
After cooling, place the films in an etching solution until the metal not protected by the photoresist lifts off.
Dip in water to stop the etching.
Rinse with acetone to remove the hardened photoresist.
Rinse with methanol and blow dry with dry nitrogen.
Drop different protein alloy solutions onto the glass surfaces.
Dry them for at least 12 hr to obtain protein alloy films on the glasses.
Peel off the protein alloy films with the thin metal patterns from the glass substrates using forceps.
Place dry films into a 60 °C vacuum oven (25 kPa) with a water dish on the bottom of the chamber.
Pump out air in the oven and let water vapors anneal samples for at least 2 hr.
Release the vacuum and peel off the water insoluble film from the substrate using forceps.
Test electrical qualities of metal patterns on protein alloy films such as electrical resistance.
Compare electrical qualities to original patterns on glass.
Dissolve or disperse the pharmaceutical compounds into an aqueous solution.
Use ultrasound or vortex to homogeneously mix the pharmaceutical compounds with water.
If the compounds are not water soluble, disperse the powders in ion-free distilled water for a homogeneous distribution.
Calculate the desired mass ratio of compounds to the protein alloy solution using volume and weight percentage calculations.
Mix the compound solution slowly with the protein alloy solution without ultrasonication or vortexing to avoid gelation.
Pour the calculated volume of mixture onto a PDMS substrate.
Dry the mixture at least 12 hours in a chemical hood to obtain a protein alloy film containing designed pharmaceutical compounds.
